To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the susceptibility of the mouse fetus to transplacently induced lung and liver tumors by MC was positively correlated with responsiveness to induction of AHH activity, and that this responsiveness was determined by the maternal genotype.

the susceptibility of the fetus to transplacently administered carcinogens is positively correlated with its ability to metabolize them, and that the susceptibility of a fetus to carcinogens is positively associated with the susceptibility of its mother.
fetal mouse susceptibility to trans-placental lung carcinogenesis by MC is determined by both maternal and fetal genetic responsiveness to induction of the Ah receptor.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of metabolic activation and detoxication of carcinogens in transplacently-induced lung and liver cancer in mice.
the mechanisms by which environmental carcinogens may induce fetal cancer.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the fetal mouse is more susceptible to transplacently-induced carcinogenesis by MC than the adult mouse, and that this is related to its ability to metabolize the carcinogen to an active form.
the fetal genotype for responsiveness in aromatic hydrocarbon metabolism is an important modulator of fetal susceptibility in transplacenta carcinogenesis.
in this system the susceptibility to transplacenetal carcinogenesis of the fetal mouse is positively correlated with the responsiveness of fetal tissue to induction of aromatic metabolism.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the AhbAhd fetus is more susceptible to MC-induced carcinogenesis than is the AhdAhd fetus, that the (C57 X DBA)2F1 fetus is more susceptible than is the DBA fetus, that maternal responsiveness to induction of Ah metabolism is not a determinant of fetal susceptibility to carcinogenesis, and that the fetal phenotype for induction of Ah metabolism, as determined by fetal genotype, is a determinant of fetal carcinogenic risk.
fetal susceptibility to transplacentally administered MC is positively correlated with fetal ability to activate the carcinogen to a proximate form.

the susceptibility to transplacentally induced lung cancer is determined by both maternal and fetal genotypes for responsiveness to aromatic hydrocarbon induction, and that the susceptibility to liver cancer is determined by fetal genotype alone.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the fetus is not a blank slate.
fetal tissue metabolism is an important determinant of fetal carcinogenic risk.
the fetus is not a passive target of carcinogens, but rather is an active participant, with the potential to modify its own risk of carcinogenesis by the induction of its own metabolic machinery.
